claim: Plants coordinate the polarity of hundreds of cells during vein formation.
source: Plants coordinate the polarity of hundreds of cells during vein formation, but how they do so is unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that the study investigates.

claim: The prevailing hypothesis proposes that GNOM positions PIN-FORMED auxin transporters to the correct side of the plasma membrane.
source: The prevailing hypothesis proposes that GNOM, a regulator of membrane trafficking, positions PIN-FORMED auxin transporters to the correct side of the plasma membrane
evidence: This is presented as the current hypothesis in the field, citing established scientific understanding.

claim: The prevailing hypothesis proposes that cell-to-cell polar transport of auxin coordinates tissue cell polarity and induces vein formation.
source: the resulting cell-to-cell, polar transport of auxin would coordinate tissue cell polarity and induce vein formation.
evidence: This is presented as part of the prevailing hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Vein formation occurs in the absence of PIN-FORMED or any other intercellular auxin-transporter.
source: we find that vein formation occurs in the absence of PIN-FORMED or any other intercellular auxin-transporter
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: The residual auxin-transport-independent vein-patterning activity relies on auxin signaling.
source: that the residual auxin-transport-independent vein-patterning activity relies on auxin signaling
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic analysis in the Results section.

claim: A GNOM-dependent signal acts upstream of both auxin transport and signaling to coordinate tissue cell polarity and induce vein formation.
source: that a GNOM-dependent signal acts upstream of both auxin transport and signaling to coordinate tissue cell polarity and induce vein formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic epistasis analysis in the Results section.

claim: In animals, coordination of tissue cell polarity requires direct cell-cell communication and often cell movements.
source: In animals, the coordination of this tissue cell polarity requires direct cell-cell communication and often cell movements (Goodrich and Strutt, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goodrich and Strutt, 2011.

claim: Direct cell-cell communication and cell movements are precluded in plants by a wall that holds cells apart and in place.
source: both of which are precluded in plants by a wall that holds cells apart and in place
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of plant cell biology.

claim: Tissue cell polarity is coordinated differently in plants than in animals.
source: therefore, tissue cell polarity is coordinated differently in plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between plant and animal cells.

claim: The formation of plant veins is an expression of coordination of tissue cell polarity.
source: The formation of plant veins is an expression of such coordination of tissue cell polarity
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: PIN1 protein catalyzes cellular efflux of auxin.
source: PIN-FORMED1 (PIN1) protein of Arabidopsis (Gälweiler et al., 1998), which catalyzes cellular efflux of the plant signal auxin (Petrásek et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gälweiler et al., 1998 and Petrásek et al., 2006.

claim: Over time, PIN1 expression becomes gradually restricted to the file of cells that will form the midvein.
source: over time, however, PIN1 expression becomes gradually restricted to the file of cells that will form the midvein.
evidence: This is based on cited observations from previous studies.

claim: PIN1 localization at the plasma membrane of inner cells is initially isotropic.
source: PIN1 localization at the PM of the inner cells is initially isotropic
evidence: This is based on observations described in the Introduction.

claim: As PIN1 expression becomes restricted to the site of midvein formation, PIN1 localization becomes polarized.
source: but as PIN1 expression becomes restricted to the site of midvein formation, PIN1 localization becomes polarized
evidence: This is based on observations described in the Introduction.

claim: In cells surrounding the developing midvein, PIN1 localization gradually changes from isotropic to medial to mediobasal.
source: in the cells surrounding the developing midvein, PIN1 localization gradually changes from isotropic to medial, that is toward the developing midvein, to mediobasal
evidence: This is based on observations described in the Introduction.

claim: In cells of the developing midvein, PIN1 becomes uniformly localized toward the base of the leaf primordium.
source: in the cells of the developing midvein, PIN1 becomes uniformly localized toward the base of the leaf primordium, where the midvein will connect to the pre-existing vasculature.
evidence: This is based on observations described in the Introduction.

claim: Auxin-induced PIN1 expression domains become restricted to the sites of auxin-induced vein formation.
source: such domains become restricted to the sites of auxin-induced vein formation, and PIN1 localization becomes polarized toward the pre-existing vasculature (Scarpella et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scarpella et al., 2006.

claim: Chemical inhibition of auxin transport delays both the restriction of PIN1 expression domains and the polarization of PIN1 localization.
source: Both the restriction of PIN1 expression domains and the polarization of PIN1 localization are delayed by chemical inhibition of auxin transport (Scarpella et al., 2006; Wenzel et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scarpella et al., 2006 and Wenzel et al., 2007.

claim: Chemical inhibition of auxin transport induces vein pattern defects similar to, though stronger than, those of pin1 mutants.
source: which induces vein pattern defects similar to, though stronger than, those of pin1 mutants (Mattsson et al., 1999; Sieburth, 1999; Sawchuk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mattsson et al., 1999; Sieburth, 1999; and Sawchuk et al., 2013.

claim: Available evidence suggests that auxin coordinates tissue cell polarity to induce vein formation.
source: Therefore, available evidence suggests that auxin coordinates tissue cell polarity to induce vein formation
evidence: This is inferred from the cited observations.

claim: The coordinative and inductive property of auxin depends on the function of PIN1 and possibly other PIN genes.
source: and that the coordinative and inductive property of auxin depends on the function of PIN1 and possibly other PIN genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited observations.

claim: The current hypothesis is that GNOM controls the cellular localization of PIN1 and possibly other auxin transporters.
source: the current hypothesis is that the GNOM (GN) guanine-nucleotide exchange factor for ADP-ribosylation-factor GTPases, which regulates vesicle formation in membrane trafficking, controls the cellular localization of PIN1 and possibly other auxin transporters
evidence: This is presented as the current hypothesis, citing reviews (Berleth et al., 2000; Richter et al., 2010; Nakamura et al., 2012; Linh et al., 2018).

claim: According to the current hypothesis, cell-to-cell polar transport of auxin would coordinate tissue cell polarity and control developmental processes such as vein formation.
source: the resulting cell-to-cell, polar transport of auxin would coordinate tissue cell polarity and control developmental processes such as vein formation (reviewed in, e.g., Berleth et al., 2000; Richter et al., 2010; Nakamura et al., 2012; Linh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is presented as part of the current hypothesis, citing reviews.

claim: In WT leaves, PIN1::PIN1:YFP was expressed in all the cells at early stages of tissue development.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Benková et al., 2003; Reinhardt et al., 2003; Heisler et al., 2005; Scarpella et al., 2006; Wenzel et al., 2007; Bayer et al., 2009; Sawchuk et al., 2013; Marcos and Berleth, 2014; Verna et al., 2015), in WT leaves PIN1::PIN1:YFP was expressed in all the cells at early stages of tissue development.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: Over time in WT leaves, epidermal PIN1::PIN1:YFP expression became restricted to the basalmost cells.
source: Over time, epidermal expression became restricted to the basalmost cells
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Over time in WT leaves, inner tissue PIN1::PIN1:YFP expression became restricted to developing veins.
source: and inner tissue expression became restricted to developing veins (Figure 1A–J).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In gn leaves, PIN1::PIN1:YFP was expressed in all the cells at early stages of tissue development.
source: In gn leaves too, PIN1::PIN1:YFP was expressed in all the cells at early stages of tissue development
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Over time in gn leaves, epidermal PIN1::PIN1:YFP expression became restricted to the basalmost cells.
source: and over time epidermal expression became restricted to the basalmost cells
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In gn leaves, inner tissue PIN1::PIN1:YFP expression failed to become restricted to developing veins and remained nearly ubiquitous even at very late stages of leaf development.
source: however, inner tissue expression failed to become restricted to developing veins and remained nearly ubiquitous even at very late stages of leaf development (Figure 1K–O).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In WT leaves at early stages of second loop development, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression in cells of the second loop was mainly localized to the side of the plasma membrane facing the midvein.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Benková et al., 2003; Reinhardt et al., 2003; Heisler et al., 2005; Scarpella et al., 2006; Wenzel et al., 2007; Bayer et al., 2009; Sawchuk et al., 2013; Marcos and Berleth, 2014; Verna et al., 2015), in the cells of the second pair of vein loops ('second loop' hereafter) at early stages of its development in WT leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was mainly localized to the side of the plasma membrane (PM) facing the midvein
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: In WT leaves at early stages of second loop development, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression in inner cells flanking the developing loop was mainly localized to the side of the PM facing the developing loop.
source: in the inner cells flanking the developing loop, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was mainly localized to the side of the PM facing the developing loop
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: In WT leaves at early stages of second loop development, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression in inner cells further away from the developing loop was localized isotropically at the PM.
source: and in the inner cells further away from the developing loop, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was localized isotropically at the PM (Figure 1C,P).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: At later stages of second-loop development in WT leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was localized to the side of the PM facing the midvein.
source: At later stages of second‐loop development, by which time PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression had become restricted to the cells of the developing loop, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was localized to the side of the PM facing the midvein (Figure 1D,T).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At early stages of development of the tissue corresponding to the second loop in gn leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP was expressed uniformly in the outermost inner tissue.
source: At early stages of development of the tissue that in gn leaves corresponds to that from which the second loop forms in WT leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP was expressed uniformly in the outermost inner tissue
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At early stages of development of the tissue corresponding to the second loop in gn leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression was localized isotropically at the PM in the outermost inner tissue.
source: and expression was localized isotropically at the PM (Figure 1Q,R).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At early stages of development of the tissue corresponding to the second loop in gn leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP was expressed more heterogeneously in the innermost inner tissue.
source: PIN1::PIN1:GFP was expressed more heterogeneously in the innermost inner tissue
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At early stages of development of the tissue corresponding to the second loop in gn leaves, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression remained localized isotropically at the PM in the innermost inner tissue, except in cells near the edge of higher-expression domains.
source: but expression remained localized isotropically at the PM, except in cells near the edge of higher-expression domains: in those cells, localization of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression at the PM was weakly polar, but such weak cell polarities pointed in seemingly random directions (Figure 1Q,S).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At late stages of gn leaf development, heterogeneity of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression had spread to the outermost inner tissue.
source: At late stages of gn leaf development, heterogeneity of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression had spread to the outermost inner tissue
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At late stages of gn leaf development, PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression remained localized isotropically at the PM in the outermost inner tissue, except in cells near the edge of higher-expression domains where localization was weakly polar in seemingly random directions.
source: but expression remained localized isotropically at the PM, except in cells near the edge of higher-expression domains: in those cells, localization of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression at the PM was weakly polar, but such weak cell polarities pointed in seemingly random directions (Figure 1U,V).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At late stages of gn leaf development, heterogeneity of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression in the innermost inner tissue had become more pronounced.
source: Heterogeneity of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression in the innermost inner tissue had become more pronounced at late stages of gn leaf development
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At late stages of gn leaf development, the weakly polar localization of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression at the PM had spread to the center of the higher-expression domains in the innermost inner tissue.
source: and the weakly polar localization of PIN1::PIN1:GFP expression at the PM had spread to the center of the higher-expression domains (Figure 1U,W)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At late stages of gn leaf development, weak cell polarities in the innermost inner tissue still pointed in seemingly random directions.
source: nevertheless, such weak cell polarities still pointed in seemingly random directions (Figure 1U,W).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Both restriction of PIN1 expression domains and coordination of PIN1 polar localization occur only to a very limited extent or fail to occur altogether during gn leaf development.
source: In conclusion, both restriction of PIN1 expression domains and coordination of PIN1 polar localization occur only to a very limited extent or fail to occur altogether during gn leaf development
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The observation that restriction of PIN1 expression domains and coordination of PIN1 polar localization occur only to a very limited extent or fail to occur altogether during gn leaf development is consistent with the current hypothesis of how auxin coordinates tissue cell polarity to induce vein formation.
source: which is consistent with the current hypothesis of how auxin coordinates tissue cell polarity to induce vein formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and the stated hypothesis.

claim: WT Arabidopsis grown under normal conditions forms separate leaves whose vein networks are defined by at least four reproducible features.
source: WT Arabidopsis grown under normal conditions forms separate leaves whose vein networks are defined by at least four reproducible features (Telfer and Poethig, 1994; Nelson and Dengler, 1997; Kinsman and Pyke, 1998; Candela et al., 1999; Mattsson et al., 1999; Sieburth, 1999; Steynen and Schultz, 2003; Sawchuk et al., 2013; Verna et al., 2015) (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the leaves of gn-18, closed loops were often replaced by open loops.
source: In the leaves of the new weak allele gn‐18 (Supplementary file 1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) closed loops were often replaced by open loops, that is loops that contact the midvein or other loops at only one of their two ends
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the leaves of gn-18, veins were often replaced by vein fragments.
source: and veins were often replaced by 'vein fragments', that is stretches of vascular elements that fail to contact other stretches of vascular elements at either one of their two ends (Figure 2C–E,N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Loops were open and veins were fragmented in the leaves of both gnfwr and gnB/E.
source: Loops were open and veins were fragmented also in the leaves of both gnfwr (Okumura et al., 2013) and gnB/E (Geldner et al., 2004) (Figure 2N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and citations.

claim: The vein network of gnB/E leaves was denser.
source: In addition, the vein network of gnB/E leaves was denser (Figure 2F,N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The vein network was denser in all the leaves of the intermediate alleles gnR5, gnvan7 and gnvan7+fwr;gn-13.
source: The vein network was denser also in all the leaves of the intermediate alleles gnR5 (Geldner et al., 2004), gnvan7 (Koizumi et al., 2000) and gnvan7+fwr;gn‐13, in which we had combined the van7 and fwr mutations (Supplementary file 1) (Figure 2G,N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and citations.

claim: In the leaves of gnR5, gnvan7 and gnvan7+fwr;gn-13, the veins were thicker.
source: However, in the leaves of these backgrounds, unlike in those of gnB/E, the veins were thicker
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the leaves of gnR5, gnvan7 and gnvan7+fwr;gn-13, lateral veins failed to join the midvein but ran parallel to it to form a wide midvein.
source: lateral veins failed to join the midvein but ran parallel to it to form a 'wide midvein'
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the leaves of gnR5, gnvan7 and gnvan7+fwr;gn-13, the vein network outline was jagged because of narrow clusters of vascular elements that were oriented perpendicular to the leaf margin and that were laterally connected by veins.
source: and the vein network outline was jagged because of narrow clusters of vascular elements that were oriented perpendicular to the leaf margin and that were laterally connected by veins (Figure 2G,H,K,N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In most of the leaves of the strong alleles gnSALK_103014, gn-13 and gnemb30-8, a central, shapeless vascular cluster was connected with the basal part of the leaf by a wide midvein.
source: In most of the leaves of the strong alleles gnSALK_103014 (Okumura et al., 2013), gn‐13 and gnemb30‐8 (Franzmann et al., 1989; Moriwaki et al., 2014), a central, shapeless vascular cluster was connected with the basal part of the leaf by a wide midvein
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2 and citations.

claim: In most of the leaves of the strong alleles gnSALK_103014, gn-13 and gnemb30-8, vascular elements were oriented seemingly randomly at the distal side of the cluster and gradually more parallel to the leaf axis toward the proximal side of the cluster.
source: vascular elements were oriented seemingly randomly at the distal side of the cluster and gradually more parallel to the leaf axis toward the proximal side of the cluster (Figure 2I,L–N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the remaining leaves of gnSALK_103014, gn-13 and gnemb30-8, vascular differentiation was limited to a central, shapeless cluster of seemingly randomly oriented vascular elements.
source: In the remaining leaves of these backgrounds, vascular differentiation was limited to a central, shapeless cluster of seemingly randomly oriented vascular elements (Figure 2J,M,N; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: pin1 is the only pin single mutant with vein pattern defects.
source: pin1 is the only pin single mutant with vein pattern defects
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawchuk et al., 2013.

claim: The vein pattern defects of double mutants between pin1 and pin2, pin3, pin4, or pin7 are no different from those of pin1 single mutants.
source: and the vein pattern defects of double mutants between pin1 and pin2, pin3, pin4, or pin7 are no different from those of pin1 single mutants (Sawchuk et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawchuk et al., 2013.

claim: PIN3::PIN3:GFP, PIN4::PIN4:GFP, and PIN7::PIN7:GFP are all expressed in both epidermal and inner cells of the developing leaf.
source: whose translational fusions to GFP (Zadnikova et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2016; Belteton et al., 2018) (Supplementary file 1) are all expressed, as are translational fusions of PIN1 to GFP (Benková et al., 2003; Heisler et al., 2005; Scarpella et al., 2006; Wenzel et al., 2007; Bayer et al., 2009; Marcos and Berleth, 2014), in both epidermal and inner cells of the developing leaf (Figure 3A,C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and citations.

claim: The vein patterns of most of the pin1 leaves were abnormal.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Sawchuk et al., 2013; Verna et al., 2015), the vein patterns of most of the pin1 leaves were abnormal (Figure 3F,G,L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and citations.

claim: pin3;pin4;pin7 embryos were viable and developed into seedlings.
source: pin3;pin4;pin7 (pin3;4;7 hereafter) embryos were viable and developed into seedlings (Supplementary file 2A) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The vein patterns of pin3;4;7 were no different from those of WT.
source: whose vein patterns were no different from those of WT (Figure 3L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: pin1,3;4;7 embryos were viable.
source: pin1,3;4;7 embryos were also viable (Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2B.

claim: pin1,3;4;7 embryos developed into seedlings.
source: and developed into seedlings (Supplementary file 2C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–H)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2C and figures.

claim: The vein pattern defects of pin1,3;4;7 were more severe than those of pin1.
source: whose vein pattern defects were more severe than those of pin1 (Figure 3H–L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pin1,3;4;7, vascular elements were still aligned along the length of the vein as in WT.
source: however, as in WT, in pin1,3;4;7 vascular elements were still aligned along the length of the vein (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: pin2;3;4;7 embryos were viable and developed into seedlings.
source: pin2;3;4;7 embryos were viable and developed into seedlings (Supplementary file 2A) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The vein patterns of pin2;3;4;7 were no different from those of WT.
source: whose vein patterns were no different from those of WT (Figure 3L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: pin1,3;2;4;7 embryos were viable.
source: pin1,3;2;4;7 embryos were also viable (Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2B.

claim: pin1,3;2;4;7 embryos developed into seedlings.
source: and developed into seedlings (Supplementary file 2C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–H)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2C and figures.

claim: The vein pattern defects of pin1,3;2;4;7 were no different from those of pin1,3;4;7.
source: whose vein pattern defects were no different from those of pin1,3;4;7 (Figure 3L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: PIN6 and PIN8 provide vein patterning functions that overlap with those of PIN1.
source: PIN6 and PIN8, but not PIN5, provide vein patterning functions that overlap with those of PIN1 (Sawchuk et al., 2013; Verna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sawchuk et al., 2013 and Verna et al., 2015.

claim: The vein pattern of pin6;8 was no different from that of WT.
source: As previously reported (Sawchuk et al., 2013), the vein pattern of pin6;8 was no different from that of WT (Figure 3O; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and citation.

claim: pin1,3,6;4;7;8 embryos were viable.
source: pin1,3,6;4;7;8 embryos were viable (Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2B.

claim: pin1,3,6;4;7;8 embryos developed into seedlings.
source: and developed into seedlings (Supplementary file 2C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–H)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2C and figures.

claim: PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7 provide no nonredundant function in vein patterning but collectively contribute to PIN1-dependent vein patterning.
source: In conclusion, PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7 provide no nonredundant function in vein patterning but collectively contribute to PIN1‐dependent vein patterning
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data presented.

claim: PIN2 seems to have no function in vein patterning.
source: PIN2 seems to have no function in this process
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data presented.

claim: The auxin-transport pathway mediated by PIN1, PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7, and that mediated by PIN6 and PIN8 provide overlapping functions in vein patterning.
source: and the auxin‐transport pathway mediated by PIN1, PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7, and that mediated by PIN6 and PIN8 provide overlapping functions in vein patterning.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data presented.

claim: Loss of PIN-dependent vein-patterning function fails to lead to defects that fall within the vascular phenotype spectrum of gn.
source: Most important, loss of PIN‐dependent vein-patterning function fails to lead to defects that fall within the vascular phenotype spectrum of gn.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of phenotypes.

claim: PM-PIN proteins catalyze cellular auxin efflux.
source: Because PM‐PIN proteins catalyze cellular auxin efflux (Chen et al., 1998; Petrásek et al., 2006; Yang and Murphy, 2009; Zourelidou et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The vein patterns of pin1,3;4;7 lacked all the characteristic defects induced in WT by NPA.
source: The vein patterns of pin1,3;4;7 lacked all the characteristic defects induced in WT by NPA (Figure 4A,B,D,E,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: NPA induced characteristic defects in pin1,3;4;7.
source: However, such defects were induced in pin1,3;4;7 by NPA (Figure 4F,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: pin1,3;4;7 has residual NPA-sensitive vein-patterning activity.
source: suggesting that this background has residual NPA‐sensitive vein‐patterning activity.

claim: The vein pattern defects induced in WT or pin1,3;4;7 by NPA were no different from those of pin1,3,6;4;7;8.
source: The vein pattern defects induced in WT or pin1,3;4;7 by NPA were no different from those of pin1,3,6;4;7;8 (Figure 4C,D–F,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: No additional defects were induced in pin1,3,6;4;7;8 by NPA.
source: Because no additional defects were induced in pin1,3,6;4;7;8 by NPA (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The residual NPA-sensitive vein-patterning activity of pin1,3;4;7 is provided by PIN6 and PIN8.
source: the residual NPA‐sensitive vein‐patterning activity of pin1,3;4;7 is provided by PIN6 and PIN8.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and NPA treatment data.

claim: Growth in the presence of NPA phenocopies defects of loss of PIN-dependent vein patterning function.
source: In conclusion, growth in the presence of NPA phenocopies defects of loss of PIN‐dependent vein patterning function
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented.

claim: In the absence of PIN-dependent vein patterning function, any residual NPA-sensitive vein-patterning activity becomes inconsequential.
source: in the absence of this function, any residual NPA‐sensitive vein‐patterning activity — if existing — becomes inconsequential
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented.

claim: Neither loss of PIN-dependent vein-patterning function nor loss of NPA-sensitive vein-patterning activity leads to defects that fall within the vascular phenotype spectrum of gn.
source: and neither loss of PIN‐dependent vein‐patterning function nor loss of NPA‐sensitive vein‐patterning activity leads to defects that fall within the vascular phenotype spectrum of gn.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Cellular auxin efflux is catalyzed by the PM-localized ABCB1 and ABCB19 proteins.
source: Cellular auxin efflux is catalyzed not only by PM‐PIN proteins but by the PM‐localized ATP‐BINDING CASSETTE B1 (ABCB1) and ABCB19 proteins (Geisler et al., 2005; Bouchard et al., 2006; Petrásek et al., 2006; Blakeslee et al., 2007; Yang and Murphy, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: ABCB1::ABCB1:GFP and ABCB19::ABCB19:GFP are expressed at early stages of leaf development.
source: whose fusions to GFP (Dhonukshe et al., 2008; Mravec et al., 2008) are expressed at early stages of leaf development (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 5 and citations.

claim: The embryos of abcb1 and abcb19 were viable.
source: The embryos of abcb1 and abcb19 were viable
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2D.

claim: Approximately 15% of abcb1;19 embryos died during embryogenesis.
source: but ~15% of abcb1;19 embryos died during embryogenesis (Supplementary file 2D)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2D.

claim: The vein patterns of abcb1, abcb19, and abcb1;19 were no different from the vein pattern of WT.
source: nevertheless, the vein patterns of abcb1, abcb19, and abcb1;19 were no different from the vein pattern of WT (Figure 5E,F,I; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: ABCB1/19-mediated auxin efflux is dispensable for vein patterning.
source: suggesting that ABCB1/19‐mediated auxin efflux is dispensable for vein patterning.
